early.title: Early start
early.hint: The 5-hour window starts with your first message. If a morning task in Claude starts it, the limit resets right in the middle of your workday — use it up before the reset and get a fresh one.
early.switch_hint: The limit resets in the middle of the workday, not in the evening.
early.task_line: The task will send a short request at {task}. Set the reset 2–3 hours after you start work.
early.task_line_prev: The task will send a short request at {task} the evening before. Set the reset 2–3 hours after you start work.
early.guide_btn: Set up the task in Claude
early.prompt: Tell me one short interesting fact about cats, in one sentence.
early.g1: Open Claude (the app or claude.ai) and on the left choose Scheduled → New task → Set up manually.
early.g2: Name it {name}. Paste this into the prompt field:
early.g3: Frequency — every day, time — {task}. If you can't pick minutes, use exactly {hour}.
early.g3_prev: Frequency — every day, time — {task} (the evening before). If you can't pick minutes, use exactly {hour}.
early.g4: Model — the lightest one on the list (for example Haiku), if you can choose. Click Save.
early.alt: Or just send this message to Claude in a new chat — it will create the task itself:
early.alt_msg: Create a scheduled task “{name}”: every day at {task} my local time, send the prompt “{prompt}” Use the lightest model.
early.note: The task runs on Claude's side. The request is tiny and barely uses the limit. TokenCat sends nothing itself: it only shows whether the early start worked.
early.st.wait: The task will start the window at {task} — the reset will be at {reset}.
early.st.nodata: Expecting the reset at {reset}. I'll check once limit data arrives.
early.st.ok: It worked: the 5-hour limit will reset at {reset}.
early.st.miss: The window didn't start: it looks like the Claude task at {task} didn't run. Check it under Scheduled.
early.st.other: The reset is now at {reset}, not {want}: the window started before the task (or the task didn't run).
onb.hello_lead: A small panel that shows in real time how much of your Claude subscription limits you've used — for 5 hours and for the week — and when they reset.
onb.os_hint: We'll pick a panel style for it. You'll sign in through the claude.ai window — no keys or passwords in TokenCat.
onb.view_lead: You can change this later in settings.
onb.card_overlay: A small panel on the desktop. Movable, always in sight.
onb.card_taskbar: Two mini bars by the tray. Click for the full panel.
onb.card_menubar: The cat and percentages next to the clock. Click for the full panel.
onb.login_lead: A claude.ai window will open — sign in as usual. It closes by itself afterwards, and TokenCat keeps the session in the system's secure storage.
onb.logged: Done! You're signed in to claude.ai.
onb.login_closed: The sign-in window was closed. You can try again or skip.
onb.new_acc_lead: Sign in to another claude.ai account — this panel will have its own limits. The sign-in window opens fresh; your first account won't be affected.
onb.early_lead: The 5-hour window starts with your first message. Start it early in the morning and the limit resets in the middle of your workday: use it up before the reset, then get a fresh one.
onb.early_yes: Worth turning on if you work with Claude during the day and hit the 5-hour limit.
onb.early_no: You can skip it if you rarely reach the limit. The request is tiny and barely uses it.
onb.done_lead: The panel will appear in the top right corner of the screen. Drag it with the mouse, double-click to refresh, right-click for the menu.

facts: Cats sleep 12–16 hours a day on average — about two thirds of their lives.
Purring sounds at around 25–150 Hz, and cats purr not only when happy but also to calm themselves down.
Adult cats meow almost only for humans: with each other they talk through scent, posture and eye contact.
A cat has 32 muscles in each ear and can turn its ears almost 180 degrees.
The pattern on every cat's nose is unique, like a human fingerprint.
Cats can't taste sweetness: the gene for that taste receptor doesn't work in them.
A cat's heart beats about 140–220 times a minute — almost twice as fast as a human's.
A cat can jump five to six times its own height.
Most cats have 18 toes: five on each front paw and four on each back paw.
Cats walk like camels and giraffes: first both right legs, then both left ones.
A cat's whiskers are about as wide as its body — that's how it knows whether it fits through a gap.
Cats see six times better than humans in the dark thanks to a reflective layer behind the retina.
A slow blink is a sign of trust in cats. Blink slowly at a cat and it may blink back.
Kittens are born with blue eyes; their real color appears after a few weeks.
Cats were domesticated about 10,000 years ago in the Middle East — they came to people on their own to catch mice.
A cat's rough tongue is covered with tiny keratin hooks — a comb and a spoon in one.
Cats spend up to half of their waking time grooming.
Calico cats are almost always female: the orange and black colors are carried on the X chromosome.
Orange cats are more often boys — about 80% of orange cats are male.
Cats can tell their owner's voice from strangers', even when they pretend not to hear.
An ordinary house cat can run at about 45 km/h over a short distance.
A cat's collarbones float freely, so it can squeeze through any gap its head fits through.
Cats' sense of smell is about 14 times better than ours.
Cats have a Jacobson's organ on the roof of the mouth: opening the mouth in a “grimace”, a cat “tastes” a smell.
The tail helps a cat keep its balance on narrow surfaces and during jumps.
Cats land on their feet thanks to the righting reflex, which kittens develop by about seven weeks.
The oldest known cat, Creme Puff from Texas, lived to 38.
In 1963 a cat named Félicette flew on a rocket and came back safely.
In ancient Egypt, killing a cat could be punished by death, and dead cats were mummified.
Cats rub against you to leave their scent: they have glands on their cheeks, chin and forehead.
Kneading is a habit from kittenhood: that's how kittens get milk flowing from their mother.
Cats see poorly right under their nose — they find close objects with their whiskers.
Cats see the world in blues and greenish yellows; red looks almost gray to them.
A moist nose helps a cat pick up scents better.
Cats sweat only through their paw pads — after stress they may leave damp paw prints.
Kittens start purring as early as their second day of life.
A cat raises its tail straight up when it's happy to see you: that's cat for “hi”.
Maine Coons are among the largest house cats: some males weigh over 10 kg.
Sphynx cats aren't completely bald — their skin is covered with soft fuzz, like a peach.
Cats can make about a hundred different sounds; dogs make about ten.
Ear tufts on lynxes and Maine Coons help direct sound into the ear.
Cats don't scratch out of spite: it renews their claws and leaves a mark.
Outdoor cats hunt 10–20 times a day on average.
Cats nap lightly: even asleep, their ears keep catching sounds.
Cats feel floor vibrations through their paws and can sense footsteps before they hear them.
A cat hears sounds up to 64 kHz — far higher than a human (about 20 kHz).
Scottish Folds owe their ears to one cat — Susie, found in 1961.
On Japan's Aoshima island, cats outnumber people about ten to one.
About 50 cats officially serve at the Hermitage museum, guarding it from rodents since the 18th century.
Cats see best at twilight: their vision is tuned to dawn and dusk — hunting time.
A kitten opens its eyes about 7–10 days after birth.
Cats drink by touching the water with the tip of the tongue: a little column rises and the cat catches it.
Cats dislike water partly because wet fur gets heavy and stops keeping them warm.
The Turkish Van is a breed that loves to swim.
A cat can rotate its hind paws claws-backward — that's why climbing up is easy and climbing down is awkward.
Cats prefer to eat little and often: in the wild that's 8–12 small “mouse” meals a day.
When a cat shows its belly, it's a sign of trust — but not always an invitation to rub it.
Cats can add a “pleading” note to their purr that sounds like a baby's cry — people respond to it readily.
Cats remember places and routes for years and can find their way home from miles away.
Cats have a favorite paw: males are more often left-pawed, females right-pawed.
